name: VoiceAssistant-Eval
description: A comprehensive benchmark for evaluating AI assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing. It comprises 10,497 curated examples spanning 13 task categories, including natural sounds, music, spoken dialogue, multi-turn dialogue, role-play imitation, and multimodal image-audio understanding.
creator: Ke Wang; Houxing Ren; Zimu Lu; Mingjie Zhan; Hongsheng Li
citeAs: Ke Wang, Houxing Ren, Zimu Lu, Mingjie Zhan, Hongsheng Li. VOICEASSISTANT-EVAL: Benchmarking AI Assistants Across Listening, Speaking, and Viewing. arXiv:2509.22651v1, 2025.
rai:dataCollection: When collecting test data, the authors first extracted diverse visual and auditory inputs from 37 datasets, and elsewhere state the benchmark uses 47 source datasets in total. The benchmark is organized into three subsets: Listening, Speaking, and Viewing. Listening source data were collected from 23 audio understanding datasets; Speaking source data came from 22 datasets including 11 text datasets and 11 audio datasets; Viewing used MMMU as the source dataset. For role-play, they used role profiles and question texts from RoleBench, selected 100 distinct roles, and collected three representative audio clips per role. Text instructions were replaced with synthesized speech instructions using three TTS models. A multi-stage curation process included deduplication, filtering incomplete or inappropriate items, categorization into 13 task categories, and balanced sampling, resulting in 10,497 high-quality samples.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: They filter out incomplete or inappropriate items, including cases with missing or broken audio or images, corrupted images, and silent audio. Approximately 10% of candidates are removed during validation/curation.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data come from existing datasets: 23 audio understanding datasets for Listening, 22 datasets for Speaking (11 text and 11 audio datasets), MMMU for Viewing, and RoleBench for role-play texts and profiles. The benchmark includes extracted visual and auditory inputs, question texts, role audio clips, synthesized spoken prompts, images, and reference answers.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors de-duplicated content using lexical overlap and edit-distance/Levenshtein distance matching, manually reviewed suspected duplicates, mapped remaining examples to 13 task categories based primarily on source metadata, and applied balanced sampling to equalize category representation. They also rewrote question texts for TTS suitability, replaced image tokens with descriptive phrases, rephrased multiple-choice options for readability, and converted collected text instructions into audio.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Preprocessing included converting collected text instructions into audio; replacing special image tokens such as '<image1>' with descriptive phrases; rewriting text with Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct so numbers and mathematical expressions are read accurately by TTS; rephrasing multiple-choice options for readability; evaluating synthesized speech with UTMOS Strong and regenerating clips until the score exceeded 3.8; transcribing synthesized audio with Whisper-Large-v3 and selecting the sample with the lowest word error rate; deduplicating questions; excluding corrupted images, silent audio, ill-posed prompts, demonstrably incorrect answers, and incomplete or unsuitable instances.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Manual curation was performed through a lightweight web-based curation tool. Curators reviewed candidate items consisting of a unique ID, metadata, raw prompt, reference answers, and associated media, then assigned a Good or Bad verdict with optional notes. Manual review proceeded in three passes: media integrity, task well-posedness, and answer validity. For evaluation, human judges independently evaluated 10% of Qwen2.5-Omni-7B responses from each of the 13 tasks, totaling 1,050 examples.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Suspected duplicates were manually reviewed and removed after automatic flagging. The curation tool exported an audit log with item IDs, curator decisions, and timestamps. For evaluation validation, 1,050 sampled responses were independently evaluated by human judges, and agreement with automated evaluation using gpt-oss-20b was analyzed via Pearson correlation coefficients and agreement rates. The paper also reports repeated-run stability analysis and statistical significance testing.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, UTMOS Strong, Whisper-Large-v3, gpt-oss-20b, emotion2vec, Wespeaker
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset and evaluation code will be publicly available. The authors state they will maintain a data governance process for auditing and removal and reserve the right to update assets if consent or licensing concerns arise. They also mention providing safety cards describing acceptable use, known risks, and red-team tests for voice cloning abuse.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The benchmark includes role-play voice imitation and speaker similarity evaluation, using multiple voice profiles and role audio clips. The paper discusses identifiable speakers, consent, provenance, anti-impersonation safeguards, privacy violations, and unequal performance across demographics. It also mentions five Chinese roles and otherwise English prompts.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states the benchmark is intended to help researchers better evaluate voice assistants and facilitate future studies. It emphasizes risks from role-play voice imitation and speaker similarity evaluation, including identity spoofing, harassment, fraud, impersonation, privacy violations, and unequal performance across demographics. The authors propose safeguards such as prohibiting training or releasing models intended to reproduce identifiable speakers without documented consent, requiring consent gating and watermarking or traceability of synthetic audio, and providing safety cards.
rai:dataBiases: The authors note that the benchmark may carry biases from its source data and design choices. Questions and contexts are drawn from academic or synthetic sources, such as existing datasets and rewritten instructions, which might not reflect the full richness or fairness concerns of real deployments. The role-play subset uses a fixed set of 100 roles that may encode stereotypes or omit important user personas. They also note reliance on automated measures and GPT-based scoring may introduce noise and bias, and that the GPT judge may favor certain phrasings or overlook nuanced errors.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset may be limited in diversity; although it includes five Chinese roles in the role-play task, all other prompts and evaluations are in English, limiting generalization to more diverse linguistic settings. The evaluated model range is limited, with only one proprietary system included. The evaluation methodology relies on automated measures and GPT-based scoring, which may introduce noise and bias. The benchmark may inherit biases from source data and design choices. Task coverage is incomplete: video-audio integration and continuous audio-visual streaming are out of scope. The benchmark is offline and static, so it does not measure latency, partial utterance handling, barge-in, or error recovery. The paper also states the dataset is not supposed to be used for training models for cheating, though that risk exists.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for evaluating voice assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing, and for tracking progress toward next-generation multimodal AI assistants. The paper presents it as a benchmark for rigorous testing by researchers and practitioners. It is not supposed to be used for training models for cheating. The benchmark is also intended to support transparent, longitudinal assessment of system capabilities.
